trees.name: The Arboretum Willow Oak
trees.age_estimate: rumoured to date to the Civil War era, confirmed fully grown by the 1940s

location.address: U.S. National Arboretum, 3501 New York Avenue NE, Washington, DC (exact tree location within the grounds not confirmed this pass; ask arboretum staff or check with Friends of the National Arboretum)

trees.age_min_note: Casey Trees says local legend traces it to the Civil War (1861-65, so 160+ years), but the earliest hard evidence they cite is a 1940s photograph showing it already fully grown but visibly smaller than today. Treat 90-160 as the honest range: at least mid-20th-century, possibly older, unconfirmed beyond the photo.
verified_sources: https://caseytrees.org/2023/08/and-the-largest-tree-is/ (Casey Trees, Aug 2023, on-site measurement visit with National Arboretum staff Kevin Conrad (Supervisory Horticulturalist) and Sue Greeley (Arborist and Wildlife Manager); circumference 287in, DBH 91.40in, second-largest tree measured in the whole 2023 DC big-tree contest behind only the Battery Kemble chestnut oak (wdc_003)
trees.access: Free. U.S. National Arboretum, open to the public daily (check usna.usda.gov for current hours), no admission fee.
trees.transport: No Metro station on site. Roughly 16 min by WMATA bus from downtown (checked by an earlier pass: Massachusetts Ave NE + 1st St NE to 21st Pl NE + Maryland Ave NE) or DC Streetcar from Union Station plus a short walk/bus leg.
trees.verify_notes: Only one independent source found this pass (Casey Trees, but it is a detailed on-site account with the Arboretum's own horticulturist and arborist as named quotes, not a press release). IMPORTANT HEALTH FLAG: per Casey Trees' 2023 visit, the tree took major damage in the 2012 derecho, was treated for carpenter oak worms (borers) in 2015, and has continued to decay and take storm damage since; the arborist's own words were 'this tree is near the end of its life,' though staff are actively extending it and prioritising visitor safety by trimming rotting branches. It IS alive as of Aug 2023 (the most recent confirmation this pass could find; no 2024/2025 update located, including no confirmation either way after DC's July 2024 derecho-strength storm). At 287in circumference / 91.40in DBH it came within 3 inches of being the single largest tree measured anywhere in DC that year, second only to the Battery Kemble chestnut oak. A local legend claims Civil War-era origin; the only hard dating evidence is a 1940s photo showing it already grown. This is a compelling but fragile story, structurally similar to the propped Washington Monument mulberry (wdc_005): a public institution visibly nursing a dying giant rather than removing it. A future pass should get the exact in-grounds location (ask staff / arboretum map) and a fresher health check before this ships without the flag, and try to find a second independent source (local news, American Forests champion tree register did not list it in this pass's search).

trees.name: The Survey Lodge Catalpas
trees.species: Catalpa (Catalpa speciosa or bignonioides, exact species not specified by either source)

location.address: In front of the Survey Lodge Ranger Station, on the oval path southwest of the Washington Monument, National Mall, Washington, DC (between the lodge's front door and the road, per National Park Trust's own visiting directions)

verified_sources: https://www.nps.gov/articles/silent-sentinels-of-storied-landscapes.htm (National Park Service, 'Silent Sentinels of Storied Landscapes', part of the 2006 HALS Witness Tree Protection Program write-up; describes catalpas northwest and southeast of Survey Lodge, possibly from the road-lining planting recorded by 1902, part of the same 24-tree survey that produced wdc_001/004/006)

https://parktrust.org/blog/youve-heard-of-the-witness-protection-program-but-have-you-heard-of-the-witness-tree-protection-program/ (National Park Trust blog, independent write-up of the same HALS programme, states the catalpas 'were planted in 1902' and gives on-site finding directions: 'right between the front door and the road')
trees.access: Free, fully public. Stand in the open on NPS parkland right by the Survey Lodge Ranger Station building (itself closed to the public, used as an NPS office), on the walking paths southwest of the Washington Monument.
trees.transport: About 10-12 min walk from Smithsonian Metro station (Blue/Orange/Silver), same approach as the nearby Washington Monument Witness Mulberry (wdc_005), roughly 250m away.
trees.verify_notes: Small ensemble of a few large catalpa trees standing together right at the Survey Lodge's front door, one obvious place to stand (per NPS: northwest and southeast of the lodge; per Park Trust: between the door and the road, so effectively flanking the entrance). Survey Lodge itself was built in 1889 as the Washington Monument's elevator boiler/steam house, is built from leftover Monument marble and granite, and is now an NPS ranger office, closed to the public, but the trees and building exterior are fully viewable from the surrounding public paths. AGE DISAGREEMENT, not silently resolved: the NPS article hedges ('could date from the turn-of-century planting project... making them significant because of their age', citing an oval road built by 1902 lined with fir, pine, crape myrtle and catalpas), while National Park Trust states flatly 'planted in 1902.' Both agree on the same approximate date and the same century-plus-of-history framing (they would have watched the Monument's first major restoration in the 1930s). No dedicated recent (post-2010) site visit or photo confirming current health was found this pass; the trees are described in both sources as thriving shade trees, no sign of decline reported anywhere. Species: neither source gives northern (Catalpa speciosa) vs southern (C. bignonioides) catalpa, worth nailing down with a photo or on-site ID before writing.

trees.name: The Willow Oak Circle
trees.age_estimate: at least 45 years, possibly around a century

location.address: South of the Vietnam Women's Memorial, Constitution Gardens, National Mall, Washington, DC (cross the grass south of the memorial to the next pathway; the circle of trees is immediately there)

verified_sources: https://www.nps.gov/articles/silent-sentinels-of-storied-landscapes.htm (National Park Service, 'Silent Sentinels of Storied Landscapes', on the same 2006 HALS Witness Tree Protection Program as wdc_001/004/006/008)

https://parktrust.org/blog/youve-heard-of-the-witness-protection-program-but-have-you-heard-of-the-witness-tree-protection-program/ (National Park Trust blog, independent write-up confirming the circle's existence, location and the same two competing planting theories, plus finding directions: 'you will find yourself accidentally standing amidst quite a large, tight circle of oak trees')
trees.access: Free, fully public. Stands in the open on NPS parkland (Constitution Gardens / West Potomac Park) just south of the Vietnam Women's Memorial, no restriction.
trees.transport: About 10 min walk from Foggy Bottom-GWU Metro (Blue/Orange/Silver) or a similar walk from the Lincoln Memorial end of the Mall.
trees.verify_notes: A genuinely singular collectible point: a tight, deliberately-planted circle of willow oaks around what was once a picnic clearing, distinct enough that both sources describe visitors 'accidentally' finding themselves standing inside it. This is an ensemble whose whole point is the ring shape, i.e. the ensemble itself is the destination, closer to the Lomanstraat-tunnel model than to an ordinary avenue. AGE IS GENUINELY UNRESOLVED, both sources say so and neither picks a winner: one theory says planted in the 1920s to ring a picnic ground (making the trees round 100 years old), the other says planted during the 1970s Constitution Gardens rehabilitation for the 1976 Bicentennial (making them only 45-55 years old). Both sources state this as an open question rather than a dispute between two sources, so deliver as flagged with the honest range 45-105 rather than picking a figure. Both agree the circle predates the Vietnam Veterans Memorial's 1982 dedication and the Vietnam Women's Memorial's 1993 dedication, so it has watched both go up regardless of which planting date is correct. No individual tree count given by either source ('several' / 'quite a large... circle'); a future pass should count them on the ground and get a photo, which would also nail the collectible-point framing (how large is 'large'?).

trees.name: The Cork Trees of the FDR Memorial
trees.age_estimate: at least 80 years as of the original 2006 HALS survey, so roughly 100 years now

location.address: Franklin Delano Roosevelt Memorial, between Room Three (the Third Term / WWII room) and the Tidal Basin waterfront, West Potomac Park, Washington, DC
location.neighbourhood: Tidal Basin / West Potomac Park (FDR Memorial)

verified_sources: https://www.nps.gov/articles/silent-sentinels-of-storied-landscapes.htm (National Park Service, 'Silent Sentinels of Storied Landscapes', same 2006 HALS Witness Tree Protection Program; states 'several Amur cork trees between room three of the FDR Memorial and the Tidal Basin with a sign stating the trees are 80 years old')

https://parktrust.org/blog/youve-heard-of-the-witness-protection-program-but-have-you-heard-of-the-witness-tree-protection-program/ (National Park Trust blog, independent corroboration, adds the detail that a 1962 NPS letter recorded no planting record for these trees and staff chose to keep them anyway for being 'very attractive old trees'; finding directions: past the visitor center restrooms, along the waterfront path, look for trees with limbs resting on the ground and two signs asking visitors not to climb them)
trees.access: Free, fully public. Stand in the open on NPS parkland within the FDR Memorial (no admission fee, open 24 hours, staffed during the day), directly on the waterfront path.
trees.transport: About 10-15 min walk from Smithsonian Metro station (Blue/Orange/Silver) along the Tidal Basin path, close to the two 1912 cherry trees (wdc_002).
trees.verify_notes: A small, named, on-site-signed cluster of Amur cork trees, sprawling and low-limbed enough that NPS puts up signs asking visitors not to climb them, which is itself a nice concrete, verifiable detail on the ground. Predates the FDR Memorial itself (dedicated 1997) by decades, since the FDR Memorial's own landscape was built around existing older plantings along what used to be a scenic drive by the Tidal Basin. GENUINE MYSTERY, not a gap in this pass's research: per a 1962 National Park Service letter (per National Park Trust; original letter not independently verified this pass, would need the NPS's own park files or the underlying HALS PDF, which is a scanned image with no extractable text this pass could OCR), the Park Service itself had no planting record for these trees even then, and kept them simply because they were 'very attractive old trees.' If the 80-years-old sign dates to the original ca. 2012 publication of the NPS article, the trees were planted around 1932; if the sign is older (installed near the FDR Memorial's 1997 dedication, which is plausible given the memorial's own age), planting could be earlier. Deliver the age as 'at least 80 years as of a sign referenced in a 2006-2012 survey' rather than inventing a precise planting year. Health: both sources describe them as characterful old trees with ground-resting limbs, no report of decline or removal.
